results.finding: Syncope during exertion is a high-risk feature requiring early in-hospital evaluation; echocardiography is recommended when structural heart disease is known or suspected, and identifies obstructive lesions such as aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, cardiac tumours and thrombi.
results.source: Brignole M et al., 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope. Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948

results.finding: When syncope is due to a structural cardiac lesion, treatment is directed at the lesion; tilt testing and exercise testing are not used to confirm a structural cause.
results.source: Brignole M et al., 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope. Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948

output.summary: ESC 2018 lists exertional syncope as high risk and recommends echocardiography when structural heart disease is suspected.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not anticoagulate as a substitute for surgical excision
Do not give vasodilators or diuretics before excision: output across a fixed outflow obstruction depends on preload and systemic resistance
Do not diagnose epilepsy or start antiseizure medication for the convulsive syncope
Do not clear him for sport before excision
required_recommendations: Diagnose exertional syncope caused by a right ventricular outflow tract mass, most likely a myxoma, with severe dynamic subpulmonic obstruction (peak gradient 90 mmHg), not epilepsy
Admit to a monitored bed with restriction of exertion until the mass is removed
Refer for urgent surgical excision of the mass during this admission by the cardiac surgical team
Send the excised mass for histopathology to confirm myxoma and exclude a malignant tumour
Screen for Carney complex given the young age and right ventricular location: skin examination for lentigines and blue naevi and an endocrine history, with PRKAR1A testing if any feature is present
Arrange echocardiographic surveillance after excision for recurrence
Advise no competitive sport and no driving until the mass has been excised and he has recovered (ESC 2018)

metadata.difficulty_description: Referred as 'new-onset seizures' because of convulsive syncope. The ECG is abnormal (RVH and strain) without a primary arrhythmia, and the diagnosis (an obstructing RV outflow tract mass) appears only on echocardiography, then cardiac MRI. patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 22-year-old male university student who presents to the emergency department after collapsing during a pickup basketball game approximately 45 minutes prior to arrival. His roommate, who witnessed the event, reports that Mr. Mehta suddenly went pale, appeared to 'lock up' with brief bilateral upper extremity stiffening lasting approximately 5-8 seconds, and then fell to the ground. There was no tonic-clonic activity, tongue biting, or urinary incontinence. The patient regained consciousness within 30 seconds and was confused for approximately one minute before returning to his baseline. Emergency medical services were called and the patient was transported to the ED. The patient reports a similar episode three weeks ago while climbing stairs rapidly in his dormitory building. During that episode, he felt a sudden 'rushing' sensation in his chest followed by tunnel vision, then woke up on the landing with a bruise on his forehead. He did not seek medical attention at that time, attributing it to dehydration and stress from exams. Over the past 4-6 months, the patient has noticed progressive exercise intolerance, becoming short of breath during activities that previously did not trouble him. He stopped playing competitive soccer approximately 4 months ago because he could not keep up. He also reports occasional palpitations described as 'fluttering' in his chest, particularly with exertion. He denies any episodes of syncope at rest, chest pain, or orthopnea. He denies any recent viral illness, fever, weight loss, night sweats, or joint pains. He has not traveled recently and denies any tick exposures. The referring emergency physician was concerned about new-onset seizures given the witnessed 'stiffening' and has referred the patient for neurological evaluation.
